statements.topic: Banning stock trading by members of Congress

said.text: "Members of Congress should not be playing the stock market while we make federal policy and have extraordinary access to confidential information." He pledged a ban as a 2020 candidate and placed his own portfolio in a blind trust in 2021.

src.t: Ossoff press release

did.text: Sponsored the Ban Congressional Stock Trading Act (2022, reintroduced 2023). On Sept. 30, 2026 he voted NO on cloture for the Republican-written Stop Insider Trading Act (H.R. 7008), which Senate Democrats called "toothless" because it exempted the executive branch and which carried an attached voter-ID requirement.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-2-253; CBS News summary

statements.record: CBS News: Democrats "viewed the voter ID provision as a 'poison pill' designed to force them to oppose stock-trading restrictions."
statements.note: A long record of sponsoring a ban; opposed the 2026 Republican vehicle on stated grounds of scope and the attached voter-ID language.

said.text: In a July 2020 campaign ad Ossoff pledged to refuse corporate PAC donations.

src.t: Thomasville Times-Enterprise

did.text: FEC filings for Jan. 2025–June 2026 show about $903,000 in itemized PAC receipts: roughly 54% from other Democrats' leadership PACs and campaign committees, 23% from labor unions, 7% from ideological groups, and the rest from professional and trade associations (for example, the National Beer Wholesalers Association, Mortgage Bankers Association and National Association of Broadcasters PACs). No company-sponsored corporate PAC appears in the filings reviewed.

src.t: FEC Schedule A, line 11C (filings listed in the Funding tab)

statements.note: Consistent with the pledge as commonly defined (company PACs). He does accept trade-association and leadership-PAC money, which critics count as corporate-adjacent.

refunded.note: Refunded in full (FEC: contribution refund, Sept. 30, 2026); the FEC lists the PAC's sponsor as a corporation.

statements.topic: Immigration enforcement — the Laken Riley Act

said.text: "Laken Riley was my constituent, and her family are my constituents. And she never should have been killed. It was preventable… we're going to have to be vigilant as we move forward, that we defend our borders and enforce our immigration laws."

src.t: PolitiFact (quoting a radio interview)

did.text: Voted YES on cloture (Jan. 9, 2025) and YES on passage of S. 5 (64-35). PolitiFact rated his opponent's claim that he "voted against the Laken Riley Act" False.

src.t: Senate roll call 119-1-7

statements.note: Votes match the stated position.

ethics.title: FEC civil penalty: late refunds of excessive and prohibited 2020 contributions
ethics.summary: The FEC's Reports Analysis Division referred Jon Ossoff for Senate for failing to timely remedy $363,272.43 in excessive, prohibited and impermissible contributions received during the 2020 general and runoff elections (from individuals including foreign addresses, non-qualified PACs, LLCs, unregistered organizations and a corporation). The committee was asked about the money in March 2021 but did not complete refunds until June 2023. In a negotiated settlement (ADR 1142) the committee agreed to a $27,000 civil penalty, a written compliance policy and outside compliance training, attributing the lapse to its external compliance vendor.
ethics.outcome: $27,000 civil penalty paid; remedial compliance measures required.

sources.t: FEC ADR 1142 — RAD referral 23L-54
FEC ADR 1142 — negotiated settlement

ethics.title: Colorado ethics commission: two gift-ban violations and a contempt finding
ethics.summary: On a complaint filed by the Public Trust Institute, the Colorado Independent Ethics Commission found that then-Gov. Hickenlooper violated the state's constitutional gift ban by accepting a March 2018 flight on a private jet owned by MDC Holdings CEO Larry Mizel (fine $2,200, 4-0) and a June 2018 Maserati limousine ride at the Bilderberg conference in Turin (fine $550, 4-1). The commission also unanimously held him in contempt after he initially refused to appear at its video hearing; no additional penalty was imposed. Colorado taxpayers paid about $127,000 in attorney fees.
ethics.outcome: $2,750 in fines; contempt finding affirmed. Hickenlooper accepted the findings.

ethics.title: Late report of a stock transaction
ethics.summary: In July 2023, Toledo TV stations WTVG (13abc) and WTOL reported that Kaptur was fined $200 for a delay in reporting a stock sale, as required under the STOCK Act's periodic transaction reporting rules. The National Republican Congressional Committee cited the late filing in a memo criticizing her, according to the Washington Examiner.
ethics.outcome: Reported $200 fine; no House Ethics Committee or Office of Congressional Conduct action found.

sources.t: 13abc (WTVG)
WTOL
Washington Examiner

Establishing the Select Committee on Electoral Reform

said.text: "By preventing Members of Congress from trading stocks, receiving yearly pay raises, and turning to lobbying shortly after their term, more lawmakers will be accountable to their constituents and be in the work of governing for the right reasons." Said when she and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-IA) introduced the No Corruption in Government Act (H.R. 358).

src.t: Office of Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez

did.text: Voted YES on H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, which also included a photo voter-ID section (roll call 280, July 22, 2026); it passed the House 232-198.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 280 (2026)

statements.note: She co-introduced a congressional stock-trading ban in 2025 and voted for the House-passed ban in 2026.

said.text: "The pressure to vote in line with your party is just immense in DC." Bloomberg Government reported at the time that she voted with her party 75% of the time on party-line votes, the third-lowest rate among House Democrats.

src.t: Bloomberg Government

did.text: Voted YES on the continuing resolution that ended the 2025 government shutdown (roll call 285, Nov. 12, 2025), which passed while most House Democrats voted NO.

src.t: House Clerk, Roll Call 285 (2025)

statements.record: In her statement on that vote she said, "I'll work with whoever is necessary to reach those goals – and I don't give a damn which side of the aisle they sit on."
statements.note: Her stated willingness to break from her party matches her vote for the shutdown-ending stopgap that most House Democrats opposed.

said.text: "Our servicemembers need reliable warfighting equipment, and their lives could depend on the ability to repair that equipment quickly when the situation demands." Said when introducing the Warrior Right to Repair Act.

src.t: Office of Rep. Gluesenkamp Perez

did.text: Introduced H.R. 5155, the Warrior Right to Repair Act of 2025, as lead sponsor with bipartisan cosponsors.

src.t: GovInfo bill status, H.R. 5155

statements.record: Her office reported she also co-led the FARM Act (H.R. 5857) on farm-equipment repair with Rep. Joe Neguse in late 2025 and helped introduce the Fair Repair Act on consumer electronics in February 2026.
statements.note: Her public advocacy for right-to-repair is matched by legislation she sponsored and co-led in the 119th Congress.

statements.topic: 2025 government shutdown and ACA tax credits

said.text: "Right now, costs are too high, and healthcare costs are about to soar because of Republican's failure to renew tax credits that make healthcare more affordable for over 100,000 South Texans." Statement issued as the federal shutdown began.

src.t: Rep. Gonzalez press release

did.text: Voted NO on the continuing resolution that ended the 2025 government shutdown (House roll call 285, Nov. 12, 2025); the measure passed the House.

src.t: House Clerk roll call 285

statements.record: On Nov. 24, 2025, his office said he had signed a discharge petition to force a House vote on a three-year extension of the ACA premium tax credits.
statements.note: He tied his shutdown position to renewing the health-care tax credits, voted against the funding bill that ended the shutdown, and then backed a discharge petition seeking a vote on extending those credits.

said.text: "Across the country, redistricting has turned into a political weapon that allows both parties to choose their voters instead of the voters choosing their leaders." Said when announcing his bill to prohibit mid-decade redistricting.

src.t: Rep. Gonzalez press release

did.text: Introduced H.R. 5879, the Save American Democracy Act, which would prohibit most mid-decade congressional redistricting; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.

src.t: GovInfo bill status, H.R. 5879

statements.note: His stated opposition to mid-decade redistricting matches the bill he introduced to restrict it.

said.text: "Warrantless immigration raids on private properties are setting a dangerous, unconstitutional precedent in this country—not just for immigrant families, but for every American family." Said when introducing the Say No to Warrantless Searches Act.

src.t: Rep. Gonzalez press release

did.text: Voted YES on the Laken Riley Act (S. 5), which requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with certain crimes such as theft; it passed the House 263-156 (House roll call 23, Jan. 22, 2025).

src.t: House Clerk roll call 23

statements.record: He also introduced H.R. 4667, the VISIBLE Act (July 23, 2025), which would require immigration enforcement officers to display visible identification during public-facing enforcement actions.
statements.note: He voted to expand mandatory detention of immigrants charged with certain crimes while sponsoring bills to limit how immigration enforcement is carried out, so his record combines support for some enforcement measures with limits on others.

ethics.summary: Business Insider reported in June 2022 that Gonzalez appeared to violate the STOCK Act's disclosure requirements with a late disclosure of a mining-stock sale, and later listed him among members of Congress who violated the law's disclosure deadlines.
ethics.outcome: The trade was disclosed, late, in June 2022. No House Ethics Committee action or penalty beyond the standard late-filing process was reported in the coverage reviewed.

Keep Kids Covered Act: would provide continuous Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for certain children

statements.topic: Voter ID and the SAVE Act

said.text: "H.R. 8281 the 'SAVE Act' is an extreme attempt to suppress voting by requiring a birth certificate – not a military id or driver's license — to register to vote." From an undated constituent e-newsletter about the 2024 version of the SAVE Act, which the House passed in July 2024.

src.t: Rep. Castor e-newsletter

did.text: Voted YES on H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act (House roll call 280, July 22, 2026). The bill bars members of Congress from buying new stocks and, as passed by the House, also requires voters to show photo ID when voting in federal elections. It passed 232-198.

src.t: House Clerk roll call 280

statements.record: She voted NO on the 2025 SAVE Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote (House roll call 102, Apr. 10, 2025). ABC News reported that House Republicans added the voter-ID language to the stock-trading bill and that many Democrats objected to it.
statements.note: She opposed the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement for registering to vote but voted for a stock-trading bill that also contained a photo-ID requirement for voting; the two measures differ, and her 2024 statement singled out birth-certificate requirements rather than driver's licenses.

said.text: "Dangerous offshore drilling can devastate both our environment and our economy, posing huge risks to everything that makes Florida special." Said when introducing the bipartisan Florida Coastal Protection Act.

src.t: Rep. Castor press release

did.text: Introduced H.R. 2673, the Florida Coastal Protection Act, which would bar oil and gas exploration, development, and production in certain Outer Continental Shelf areas off Florida; it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.

src.t: GovInfo bill status, H.R. 2673

statements.note: Her stated opposition to offshore drilling near Florida matches the bill she sponsored to prohibit it.

said.text: "Ratepayers should not have to subsidize wealthy corporations' growing energy demands, especially from AI data centers." Said when announcing a bipartisan bill on data-center electricity costs.

src.t: Rep. Castor press release

did.text: Co-led the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act with Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO). The bill aims to keep households from paying higher electric bills tied to data-center development.

src.t: Rep. Castor press release

statements.record: Castor's office announced House passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act on Sept. 16, 2026.
statements.note: Her statement on data-center energy costs matches the bill she co-led, which later passed the House.

ethics.title: Late disclosure of 2021 stock purchases
ethics.summary: Business Insider listed Castor among members of Congress who violated the STOCK Act's disclosure deadlines, reporting that she "was late disclosing the purchase of tens of thousands of dollars worth of stock shares throughout 2021." The report did not include a response from her office.
ethics.outcome: The coverage reviewed reported no House Ethics Committee or Office of Congressional Ethics action.

bill.officialTitle: An act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to titles II and V of the concurrent resolution on the budget for fiscal year 2018.
bill.summary: Cuts the corporate income tax rate from 35 percent to 21 percent permanently, lowers individual income tax rates and roughly doubles the standard deduction through 2025, and sets the individual-mandate penalty to zero from 2019.

summarySrc.t: Senate roll call vote 323 (115th Congress, 1st session)

bill.voteQuestion: On the motion to recede and concur with a further amendment

codes.why: It permanently cut the corporate tax rate from 35 percent to 21 percent, and the Tax Policy Center estimates most of its benefit goes to the highest earners by 2027.

CBO estimates that zeroing out the individual-mandate penalty leaves 13 million more people uninsured in 2027 and cuts federal health spending, mostly on Medicaid and marketplace subsidies (CBO, Nov. 2017).

bill.summary: During the January 6, 2021 counting of the 2020 presidential electoral votes, Rep. Paul Gosar, Sen. provisions.fact: Stock-trading restriction: would prohibit Members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing stocks and require public notice before they may sell stocks, with violations subject to fees and divestment requirements (CRS summary, reported version).

src.t: Bill status of H.R. 7008 (119th Congress), GovInfo bill-status XML

provisions.fact: Stock-trading penalties and exemptions in the House-passed bill: violators would face a penalty of $2,000 or 10% of the transaction value, whichever is greater, plus any net gain; widely held investment funds and investments held in a trust are exempt (States Newsroom).

src.t: States Newsroom via Wisconsin Examiner (July 22, 2026)

provisions.fact: Lawmakers could keep stocks they already own; the ban applies to buying new stocks (ABC News).

provisions.fact: Voter-ID provision: House Republicans attached a voter ID requirement to the stock-trading bill; voters would have to present a current state-issued driver's license or ID card, passport, valid military or veteran ID, or tribal ID, and mail ballots would need a copy of a valid ID, the last four digits of a Social Security number with an affidavit that the voter cannot obtain a photo ID, or a notarized statement (States Newsroom).

src.t: States Newsroom via Wisconsin Examiner (July 22, 2026)

provisions.fact: Voter-ID provision: voters would have to show a valid photo identification when casting a ballot for federal office; mail-in and absentee voters could attach a photocopy of their ID, and those without ID could cast a provisional ballot (ABC News).

record.title: 2025 quorum break over mid-decade congressional redistricting
record.detail: Joined House Democrats who left Texas to deny the House a quorum and delay a vote on a new Republican-drawn congressional map (HB 4). Democrats returned on Aug. 18; the House passed the map 88–52 on Aug. 20 and it was signed on Aug. 29, 2025. A federal court blocked the map in November 2025, but the U.S. Supreme Court stayed that ruling in December 2025 and reversed it in April 2026.

ethics.title: FEC flags excess contributions to Senate campaign
ethics.summary: The Federal Election Commission sent the Talarico campaign a 24-page letter flagging contributions above federal limits from 143 donors, NOTUS reported. The campaign had received similar notices every quarter since it started. It blamed some of the excess on its online donation settings.
ethics.outcome: The campaign is refunding or reattributing the excess; refunds of $844,347 (534 refunds) were reported as of August 2026, with about $250,000 more expected. No FEC penalty or enforcement action has been reported.

record.title: Commuted 15 death sentences

record.title: Vetoed HB 10 (school vouchers and sheriff-ICE cooperation)
record.detail: Vetoed House Bill 10, which expanded Opportunity Scholarship private-school voucher funding and required sheriffs to honor ICE detainer requests for up to 48 hours; he called the vouchers 'the biggest threat to public schools in decades.' The legislature overrode the veto (House 72-44 on Nov. 19, Senate on Nov. 20, 2024).

src.t: WUNC: Gov. Cooper vetoes bill funding private school vouchers and requiring sheriffs' ICE cooperation

record.title: Vetoed SB 20 (12-week abortion limit)
record.detail: Vetoed Senate Bill 20, which reduced the abortion limit from 20 to 12 weeks with exceptions and added new requirements on providers and patients. The Republican supermajority overrode the veto on May 16, 2023, and the bill became law.

src.t: Office of the Governor: Governor Cooper Vetoes SB20

record.title: Signed Medicaid expansion (HB 76)
record.detail: Signed House Bill 76 (Access to Healthcare Options), making North Carolina the 40th state to expand Medicaid, with coverage expected to reach more than 600,000 residents; enrollment began in December 2023.

record.title: Statewide COVID-19 Stay at Home order (EO 121)
record.detail: Issued Executive Order 121, a statewide Stay at Home order requiring residents to stay home except for essential activities and limiting gatherings to 10 people, in effect from March 30 to April 29, 2020.

src.t: NC Department of Public Safety: Governor Cooper Announces Statewide Stay at Home Order Until April 29

record.title: Signed HB 142 repealing HB2 ('bathroom bill')
record.detail: Signed a negotiated compromise that repealed HB2's bathroom restrictions but made the legislature the sole authority over restroom access and barred local regulation of private employment and public accommodations until December 1, 2020.

src.t: Ballotpedia: Did Gov. Roy Cooper betray promises on HB 2 repeal?

record.title: As attorney general, dropped Duke lacrosse charges
record.detail: After taking over the prosecution from Durham DA Mike Nifong, dismissed all charges against three Duke lacrosse players and declared them innocent, citing a 'tragic rush to accuse.'

ethics.title: Atlantic Coast Pipeline mitigation fund investigation
ethics.summary: Investigators hired by the Republican-led Joint Legislative Commission on Governmental Operations concluded that Cooper improperly used his authority to secure a $57.8 million mitigation-fund commitment from pipeline developers while a state permit was pending; the report found he did not personally benefit. Cooper called the probe partisan and denied wrongdoing, and Duke Energy and state environmental officials said they did not feel coerced.
ethics.outcome: No charges or formal sanctions; the legislature redirected the fund to schools in pipeline-route counties.

WRAL: Report: Cooper didn't benefit from pipeline actions, but investigators suggest improper influence

ethics.title: Libel suit over 2000 attorney general campaign ad (Boyce & Isley v. Cooper)
ethics.summary: Lawyers Dan Boyce (Cooper's 2000 Republican opponent), Gene Boyce and the Isleys sued Cooper over a 2000 campaign ad that implied they acted unethically in seeking attorney fees in a class-action tax case. The case ran for about 14 years before settling.
ethics.outcome: Settled in April 2014 for $75,000 plus mediator fees and a written apology signed by Cooper stating that to the extent the ad implied otherwise, "we were wrong and apologize."

record.title: DISCLOSE Act of 2026 (H.R. 7802)
record.detail: Introduced the House version of the DISCLOSE Act with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse. The bill would require super PACs, dark-money groups and other organizations spending more than $10,000 on elections to disclose donors giving more than $10,000. It would also extend disclosure rules to online ads and paid social-media influencers. His office said 139 House Democrats and 47 Democratic senators joined the House and Senate versions. The sources reviewed show no committee or floor action.

src.t: Office of Rep. Chris Pappas: Pappas, Whitehouse Reintroduce Updated DISCLOSE Act (Mar. 4, 2026)

record.title: PFAS Research and Development Reauthorization Act of 2025 (H.R. 6667)

src.t: GovInfo: H.R. 6667 (IH), 119th Congress

record.detail: The Restore, Reinvest and Renew (R3) program, whose board the Lt. Governor's office lists Stratton as leading, announced $45 million in cannabis-revenue grants to 148 programs in civil legal aid, economic development, reentry, violence prevention and youth development; the JEO report puts total R3 awards through 2022 at nearly $150 million to more than 300 organizations.

src.t: Illinois R3: ICJIA Awards $45 Million in R3 Program Grants (June 23, 2022)

record.title: State ID pilot for people leaving prison
record.detail: The JEO Initiative she leads launched a State ID pilot with the Secretary of State and the Illinois Department of Corrections in December 2020; it was expanded to all IDOC facilities by 2022 and had issued over 1,400 state IDs to people returning to their communities, according to the office's 2022 annual report.

src.t: Office of the Lt. Governor: 2022 JEO Annual Report

record.title: Cannabis legalization law (HB 1438)
record.detail: Stratton backed and spoke at the signing of HB 1438, the Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, which legalized adult-use cannabis from January 1, 2020, made about 700,000 records eligible for expungement, and directed 25% of cannabis revenue to the Restore, Reinvest and Renew (R3) grant program. The governor signed the bill.

record.title: Named to lead Justice, Equity and Opportunity Initiative
record.detail: Gov. JB Pritzker's Executive Order 2019-09 created the Justice, Equity and Opportunity (JEO) Initiative to coordinate criminal justice reform across state agencies, with an emphasis on reducing the prison population; Stratton was named to lead it, with annual reports required.

record.title: HB 2663: ban on expulsions from state-funded preschool

ethics.title: Fake-ID charge at age 19
ethics.summary: At 19, Barr was charged with possessing a fake driver's license; he pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor and was ordered to perform community service. During his 2012 House race, Democrats accused him of trying to hide the record (Associated Press).
ethics.outcome: Resolved by a guilty plea and community service; the sources reviewed document no further legal or disciplinary action.

sources.t: Nastiest Congressional Race Ever in Kentucky Coming Down to the Wire (Associated Press via WKYU, Oct. 29, 2012)

ethics.title: FEC complaint over campaign disclaimers (MUR 8060)
ethics.summary: Raymond A. Lauk filed an FEC complaint against Andy Barr for Congress, its treasurer and Barr alleging a violation of the disclaimer rules for campaign communications (52 U.S.C. § 30120; 11 CFR 110.11).
ethics.outcome: Dismissed: on Jan. 10, 2024 the Commission voted 6–0 to dismiss the complaint under its prosecutorial discretion, as its Office of General Counsel recommended, and closed the file.

sources.t: FEC: MUR 8060, Andy Barr for Congress, Inc.

ethics.title: Perjury and false-statement charges (Hubbard grand jury)
ethics.summary: While a state representative, Moore was arrested in April 2014 and charged with two counts of perjury and two counts of making false statements over his January 2014 testimony to the Lee County grand jury investigating then-House Speaker Mike Hubbard. Prosecutors alleged he testified falsely about when he learned an economic-development project in Enterprise was in jeopardy; they presented recorded conversations between Moore and his primary opponent Josh Pipkin.
ethics.outcome: Acquitted: a jury found him not guilty on all charges on October 30, 2014.

items.title: Beason-Hammon Alabama Taxpayer and Citizen Protection Act (HB 56)
items.summary: Alabama's 2011 immigration enforcement law: required police to check immigration status during lawful stops when there was reasonable suspicion a person was in the country unlawfully, required schools to determine students' immigration status, and created state crimes for harboring or transporting unauthorized immigrants. cands.status: Republican nominee; won the June 2, 2026 primary with 76.1% after Sen. Steve Daines withdrew at the March 4 filing deadline and endorsed him (Montana Free Press)

statusSrc.t: Montana Free Press 2026 Election Guide: Kurt Alme

cands.since: Former U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana (2017–2020 and 2025–March 2026); stepped down to run for the Senate
cands.roles: U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana, 2025–2026 (interim from March 2025; confirmed by the Senate 51–47 in October 2025); Director, Montana Governor's Office of Budget and Program Planning (Gov. Greg Gianforte), 2020–2021; U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana, 2017–2020; First Assistant U.S. Attorney / Assistant U.S. Attorney, District of Montana, 2003–2010; Director, Montana Department of Revenue (Gov. Judy Martz), 2001–2003
cands.background: Great Falls-born lawyer with a Harvard law degree who worked in private practice, as a federal prosecutor and as president and general counsel of the Yellowstone Boys and Girls Ranch Foundation (2013–2017). He was an executive vice president at the National Christian Foundation from 2022 to 2024.
cands.term: Running for an open Senate seat

record.title: Presented Gianforte's first state budget
record.detail: As budget director, presented Gov. Greg Gianforte's proposed 2023-biennium budget: a 2.5% general-fund spending increase, a cut in the top income tax rate from 6.9% to 6.75%, a capital-gains exemption for businesses and elimination of the business equipment tax for about 4,000 businesses; MTPR reported a structural deficit of about $59 million.

src.t: MTPR: Gianforte's first budget outlines tax cuts, spending increases and deficit

record.title: Announced resignation; office prosecutions up 15%
record.detail: The U.S. Attorney's Office reported that during his tenure federal criminal prosecutions rose 15% to more than 400 defendants a year and that statewide Project Safe Neighborhoods work produced 670+ cases, 333 pounds of meth seized and 343 firearms recovered.

src.t: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Montana: U.S. Attorney Kurt Alme announces resignation

record.title: Meth prevention coalition grant
record.detail: Announced a $248,000 federal grant to Missoula Substance Abuse Connect, a coalition his office joined through Project Safe Neighborhoods with United Way, to plan methamphetamine prevention and treatment in Missoula County.

record.title: Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons initiative
record.detail: Montana was one of 11 states chosen for the Justice Department's MMIP initiative, with its first coordinator already hired; Alme was vice chair of the Attorney General's Native American Issues Subcommittee and his office ran missing-person trainings on all seven Montana reservations.

src.t: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Montana: Attorney General Barr launches national strategy on missing and murdered Indigenous people

record.title: Project Safe Neighborhoods one-year results

record.title: Launched Project Safe Neighborhoods in Billings area

ethics.title: Wyoming State Bar complaint over 2020-election statements

ethics.title: Reported apparently late stock-trade disclosures (2024–2025 trades)
ethics.summary: NOTUS reported that, based on a House Ethics Committee deadline calculator, Hern appeared to have disclosed between $4.2 million and $17.6 million in stock and corporate-security trades late. The trades ran from December 2024 into 2025, and 10 of them were 2 to 12 days past deadline; examples were a $500,001–$1 million Citigroup security sale on Dec. 3, 2024, disclosed Jan. 15, 2025, and a $250,001–$500,000 Royal Bank of Canada purchase in January 2025, disclosed Feb. 18. His office said "The filings aren't late," stating he files no later than 30 days after notification from his financial advisor and within the 45-day transaction requirement.
ethics.outcome: Disputed by Hern's office; no fine or House Ethics Committee action was reported.

ethics.title: Late disclosure of stock trades under the STOCK Act
ethics.summary: In January 2026 Letlow disclosed more than 200 stock and bond trades after the STOCK Act's 45-day reporting deadline, some more than a year late, with total value reported in ranges of roughly $225,000 to $3.3 million. Her office said a Merrill Lynch-managed discretionary account made the trades without her direction and that she self-reported the lapse in October 2025.
ethics.outcome: The House Ethics Committee waived the $200 late-filing fee on Feb. 3, 2026; no further disciplinary action has been reported.

ethics.title: FEC complaint filed by Cassidy campaign
ethics.summary: During the Republican primary, Sen. Bill Cassidy's campaign filed an FEC complaint alleging that Letlow knowingly and willfully violated federal campaign-finance law by having a fundraiser solicit unlimited super PAC contributions on her behalf. Her campaign called the complaint desperate and said the fundraiser was a private citizen working at Gov. Jeff Landry's request, not a campaign agent.
ethics.outcome: No FEC finding or resolution has been publicly reported; status pending.

cands.name: Sherrod Brown
cands.status: Democratic nominee; won the May 5, 2026 special-election primary over Ron Kincaid

statusSrc.t: Sherrod Brown wins Ohio Democratic U.S. Senate primary, set to face Jon Husted in November (Ohio Capital Journal, Marty Schladen, May 5, 2026)

cands.since: Former U.S. Senator from Ohio (2007–2025); founder of the Dignity of Work Institute (launched March 2025)
cands.roles: U.S. Senate (Ohio), 2007–2025 (chair, Senate Banking Committee, 2021–2025); U.S. House of Representatives (Ohio's 13th District), 1993–2007; Ohio Secretary of State, 1983–1991; Ohio House of Representatives, 1975–1982
cands.background: Holds a bachelor's degree in Russian studies from Yale and master's degrees in education and public administration from Ohio State, and wrote books including Myths of Free Trade (2006). After losing his 2024 re-election bid to Republican Bernie Moreno (50.1% to 46.5%), he was a spring 2025 visiting fellow at Harvard Kennedy School and founded the Dignity of Work Institute before announcing his 2026 campaign on Aug. 18, 2025.

record.title: Railway Safety Act of 2023 (S. 576)
record.detail: Sponsored, with Republican cosponsors J.D. Vance, Marco Rubio and Josh Hawley, a bill written after the February 2023 East Palestine, Ohio, derailment to require two-person crews on Class I trains, closer spacing of wayside bearing detectors, expanded hazardous-materials rules and higher fines. The Senate Commerce Committee approved it on May 10, 2023, but it did not reach the Senate floor.

src.t: GovInfo: S. 576 (IS) - Railway Safety Act of 2023

record.title: Inflation Reduction Act (H.R. 5376)

ethics.title: Late property-tax payments and duplicate owner-occupancy credit
ethics.summary: NBC News reported that Brown had paid property taxes late at least seven times on his Cleveland home since buying it in 2013, and that he claimed Ohio's owner-occupancy tax credit on both the Cleveland home and a Columbus condo, although state law allows the credit on only one property per household. Not listed because they involve no formal complaint or finding: criticism of his January 2023 appointment by Gov. Jim Pillen, whom the Ricketts family spent over $1.3 million helping elect (Nebraska Examiner, Jan. 12, 2023), and 2026 allegations by Osborn's campaign and the Nebraska Democratic Party that Ricketts was behind Democratic candidate William Forbes's primary run and later lawsuit, which his campaign denied. Senate roll-call votes were not researched, per instructions; note that rickettsforsenate.com is an opposition parody site, not his campaign site. Rechecked Nov. 14, 2026 against the Senate Ethics Committee's letters and press releases.

ethics.title: Lawsuit over his role in the 2016 death-penalty referendum
ethics.summary: On Dec. 4, 2017 the ACLU filed a state-court suit on behalf of Nebraska death-row inmates (Sandoval v. Ricketts) alleging that Ricketts and State Treasurer Don Stenberg violated the state constitution's separation of powers by proposing, financing, organizing and directing the 2016 referendum that restored the death penalty.
ethics.outcome: Lancaster County District Court dismissed the suit, and the Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed on Jan. 25, 2019, holding that the inmates had other remedies through postconviction proceedings; the court did not find wrongdoing by Ricketts.

sources.t: Nebraska Supreme Court: Sandoval v. Ricketts, 302 Neb. 138 (Jan. 25, 2019)
VICE: Nebraska's governor loves the death penalty so much it got him sued (Dec. 4, 2017)

ethics.title: NRSC complaint to the FEC over 2025 campaign spending
ethics.summary: The National Republican Senatorial Committee asked the Federal Election Commission to investigate Peltola, alleging that more than $100,000 her House campaign committee spent in 2025 — on travel, hotels, speaking trips and food delivery — amounted to personal use because she had no visible House campaign. Her campaign called it "a completely false attack by Dan Sullivan and his Washington allies in the Lower 48."
ethics.outcome: Pending; no FEC action reported. As of March 30, 2026, the FEC had only two commissioners and lacked the four votes needed for official action.

ethics.title: House Oversight and Alaska state investigations of her campaign's alleged recruiting of a second "Dan Sullivan"
ethics.summary: On Oct. 29, 2026, House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer opened an investigation into allegations, first reported by The New York Times, that Peltola's campaign recruited challengers with a name nearly identical to Sen. Dan Sullivan's to confuse voters, and asked former campaign manager Elisa Rios and Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz for transcribed interviews on Nov. 5 and 6. The same day Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged scheme violated state law and whether criminal or civil action was warranted. Peltola herself is not named as a subject. The Times quoted Rios as saying Peltola was not directly involved but was "definitely aware"; Rios later sought to retract her comments. The campaign said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race."
ethics.outcome: Open; no finding reported as of Nov. 14, 2026.

cands.roles: Colorado House of Representatives, District 32, October 2023–September 2026 (appointed by vacancy committee in 2023; elected 2024); Economist, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 2016–2018
cands.background: Attorney from Commerce City who worked as an associate attorney at the environmental law nonprofit Earthjustice and has been CEO of Climate Refarm, a nonprofit/carbon-offset venture for food growers, since 2021. record.detail: Resigned from the Colorado House, effective September 4, 2026, to focus on the congressional race. An Adams County vacancy committee will fill the seat.

record.title: Voted for 2026-27 state budget (HB26-1410)
record.detail: Voted for the $46.8 billion Long Bill, which passed the House 43-19. To close a $1.2 billion general-fund shortfall it reduced Medicaid reimbursement rates and services by $270 million, among other cuts. Bird criticized the vote during the primary; Rutinel said he "made efforts to blunt the blow of cuts to Medicaid."

src.t: The Hill: Rutinel defeats Bird in Democratic primary for battleground Colorado House seat (June 30, 2026); tally: Colorado Politics (Apr. 11, 2026)

record.title: Worker Protection Act (SB25-005)
record.detail: Voted for the collective-bargaining bill, which would have made it easier to form unions by repealing parts of Colorado's modified right-to-work law (the Labor Peace Act). It passed the House on third reading 43-22, and Gov. Jared Polis vetoed it in May 2025.

src.t: Colorado General Assembly: SB25-005 House third reading roll call (May 6, 2025)

record.title: Immigration-status civil rights bill (SB25-276)
record.detail: Voted for the bill. Among other things it bars jails from delaying release for immigration enforcement, removes the affidavit requirement for in-state tuition and ID documents, and limits information-sharing with federal immigration authorities. It passed the House 42-21 and was signed May 23, 2025. His primary opponent Shannon Bird was excused for the floor vote.

src.t: FastDemocracy: SB 25-276 House roll call; Colorado General Assembly bill page

record.title: Semiautomatic firearms permit law (SB25-003)
record.detail: Voted for the bill, which from August 1, 2026 bars buying specified semiautomatic firearms unless the buyer completes a firearm safety course and gets a sheriff-issued eligibility card, and classifies rapid-fire devices as dangerous weapons. It passed the House 36-28 and became law.

src.t: Colorado General Assembly: SB25-003 House third reading roll call (Mar. 24, 2025)

issues.label: Health coverage costs
issues.q: ACA premium subsidies and federal Medicaid spending
issues.A: Extend ACA premium subsidies and protect federal Medicaid funding
issues.B: Let enhanced ACA subsidies lapse and reduce federal Medicaid spending
issues.statement: Congress should extend the enhanced ACA premium subsidies and protect federal Medicaid funding.

issues.label: Taxes and government spending
issues.q: Tax levels and the size of government spending (federal or state)
issues.A: Raise taxes on corporations or high earners to fund public programs
issues.B: Cut taxes and cut government spending
issues.statement: Government should raise taxes on corporations or high earners to pay for public programs.

issues.label: Immigration enforcement
issues.q: Detention and enforcement of immigration law
issues.B: Limit expansions of detention and enforcement
issues.statement: The federal government should expand immigration detention and enforcement.

issues.label: Abortion
issues.q: Legal access to abortion
issues.B: Restrict abortion
issues.statement: Legal access to abortion should be protected.

issues.label: Marriage and contraception rights in law
issues.q: Writing same-sex marriage and contraception rights into law
issues.B: Oppose these bills
issues.statement: Same-sex marriage and access to contraception should be written into law.

issues.label: Guns
issues.q: Gun regulation
issues.B: Expand gun rights or oppose new restrictions
issues.statement: Lawmakers should add new gun-safety regulations.

issues.label: Climate and energy
issues.q: Climate and clean-energy policy
issues.B: Roll back or block clean-energy and climate measures
issues.statement: Government should support clean-energy and climate measures.

issues.label: Tariffs on Canada
issues.q: The 2025 emergency tariffs on Canadian imports
issues.B: End the tariff emergency
issues.leanNote: Tariffs do not map cleanly onto liberal versus conservative: free-trade conservatives and many liberals both oppose them, and the current fight is mostly over one president’s policy.
issues.statement: The 2025 emergency tariffs on Canadian imports should stay in place.

issues.label: Aid to Ukraine
issues.q: U.S. military and economic aid to Ukraine
issues.B: Oppose aid to Ukraine
issues.leanNote: Support for Ukraine aid cuts across both parties’ wings, so a Yea is not reliably the liberal or the conservative side.
issues.statement: The United States should keep funding military and economic aid to Ukraine.

issues.label: War powers (Venezuela)
issues.q: Requiring Congress to approve U.S. hostilities against Venezuela
issues.B: Leave the decision to the President
issues.leanNote: Whether to limit presidential war powers has depended on who holds the White House, so it is not a fixed liberal or conservative position.
issues.statement: U.S. military action against Venezuela should require the approval of Congress.

issues.label: 2020 election and Jan. 6
issues.q: Certifying the 2020 election and impeaching or convicting President Trump for Jan. 6
issues.A: Certify the results and hold Trump accountable
issues.B: Object to certification and oppose impeachment
issues.leanNote: Objecting to electoral votes and impeaching a president are partisan and institutional questions, not a liberal versus conservative policy position.
issues.statement: The 2020 election results should have been certified, and President Trump impeached or convicted over January 6.

issues.label: Labor and wages
issues.q: Union bargaining rights and minimum wages set by law
issues.A: Strengthen bargaining rights and raise wage floors
issues.B: Oppose these measures
issues.statement: Union bargaining rights should be strengthened and minimum wages set by law raised.

issues.label: Voter ID and proof of citizenship
issues.q: Photo ID or proof-of-citizenship requirements to vote or register
issues.B: Oppose these requirements
issues.statement: Voters should have to show photo ID or proof of citizenship to vote or register.

issues.label: Infrastructure and industrial investment
issues.q: Large federal investments such as the 2021 infrastructure law and the CHIPS Act
issues.B: Oppose them
issues.leanNote: Infrastructure and industrial-policy investment drew bipartisan support from both wings, so it is not marked.
issues.statement: Government should make large investments in infrastructure and industry, like the 2021 infrastructure law and the CHIPS Act.

issues.label: Public money for private schools
issues.q: Vouchers or education savings accounts that pay private-school costs
issues.B: Oppose them
issues.statement: Public money should help pay private-school costs, through vouchers or education savings accounts.

issues.label: Money in politics and congressional ethics
issues.q: Banning members' stock trading and lobbying after office, and overturning Citizens United
issues.A: Ban members of Congress from trading stocks and from lobbying after they leave, and amend the Constitution to overturn Citizens United
issues.B: Keep the current rules on members' stock trading, lobbying after office and campaign spending
issues.leanNote: Stock-trading and lobbying bans draw sponsors from both parties; only the Citizens United amendment splits mostly by party, so the issue is not marked liberal or conservative.
issues.statement: Congress should ban members from trading stocks and from lobbying after they leave, and overturn Citizens United.

issues.label: Flag burning and surveillance
issues.q: Whether Congress may ban flag burning, and whether the government may use facial recognition for surveillance
issues.A: Keep flag burning legal as free speech and stop government use of facial recognition
issues.B: Let Congress ban flag burning and allow government use of facial recognition
issues.statement: Flag burning should stay legal as free speech, and the government shouldn't use facial recognition for surveillance.

issues.label: Police accountability and punishment
issues.q: Qualified immunity for police, private prisons, and the death penalty for drug dealing
issues.A: End qualified immunity and federal private prisons, and don't extend the death penalty to drug dealing
issues.B: Keep qualified immunity and make dealing deadly fentanyl punishable by death
issues.statement: Police shouldn't have qualified immunity, the federal government shouldn't use private prisons, and drug dealing shouldn't carry the death penalty.

issues.label: Housing and homelessness
issues.q: Federal money for housing and homeless services, and landlords' rent-setting software
issues.A: Spend more federal money on housing and homeless services, and ban landlords' rent-setting software
issues.B: Don't expand federal housing spending or ban rent-setting software
issues.statement: The federal government should spend more on housing and homeless services, and landlords shouldn't use software that coordinates rents.

issues.label: Social Security retirement age
issues.q: Whether to raise the Social Security full retirement age
issues.A: Keep the full retirement age where it is
issues.B: Raise the full retirement age
issues.statement: The Social Security retirement age shouldn't go up.

featured.ethicsSearched: Checked court records and major news reports through October 2026 for criminal cases, civil judgments, impeachments and other formal proceedings. Complaints or reports that no official body acted on are not listed.

ethics.title: New York conviction: 34 counts of falsifying business records
ethics.summary: A Manhattan jury convicted Trump on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal a hush-money payment before the 2016 election. On January 10, 2025, Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge, which leaves the conviction on the record without jail, probation or a fine. In August 2026 a federal judge again refused to move the case to federal court, and Trump's appeal of the conviction is set for argument in New York's Appellate Division on November 5, 2026.
ethics.outcome: Convicted; sentenced to an unconditional discharge. Appeal pending.

sources.t: PBS NewsHour: Trump loses again in bid to erase his hush money conviction (Aug. 2026)
New York Sun: Trump gets his day in court to fight convictions (Oct. 2026)

ethics.title: E. Jean Carroll: sexual abuse and defamation verdict ($5 million)
ethics.summary: A federal jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll and awarded her $5 million. The appeals court upheld the verdict; the Supreme Court declined to hear Trump's appeal in June 2026 and denied rehearing on August 17, 2026, and Carroll has been paid.
ethics.outcome: Liability final; judgment paid.

sources.t: SCOTUSblog: Supreme Court will not consider $5 million verdict against Trump (June 2026)
CNBC: Supreme Court again rejects Trump bid to overturn E. Jean Carroll verdict (Aug. 17, 2026)

ethics.title: E. Jean Carroll: defamation verdict ($83.3 million)
ethics.summary: A second federal jury ordered Trump to pay Carroll $83.3 million for defaming her. The Second Circuit upheld the judgment; on July 28, 2026, Trump and the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to overturn it, arguing presidential immunity. The Court has not yet said whether it will hear the case.
ethics.outcome: Liability upheld on appeal. Supreme Court petition pending.

sources.t: SCOTUSblog: Trump asks Supreme Court to hear appeal of $83 million defamation verdict (July 2026)
CNN: Trump urges Supreme Court to overturn E. Jean Carroll's $83M defamation verdict (July 28, 2026)

ethics.title: New York civil fraud case (People v. Trump)
ethics.summary: A New York judge found that Trump and the Trump Organization fraudulently inflated the value of assets and ordered roughly $454 million in disgorgement. On August 21, 2025, the Appellate Division threw out the monetary penalty as excessive but left the fraud liability and some business restrictions in place; both sides have appealed to the New York Court of Appeals.
ethics.outcome: Fraud liability stands; the penalty was vacated. Appeal pending.

sources.t: CNN: NY appeals court voids the nearly $500 million civil fraud penalty against Trump (Aug. 21, 2025)

ethics.title: Trump Foundation: misuse of charitable funds
ethics.summary: After the New York attorney general sued, Trump admitted to misusing funds of the Donald J. Trump Foundation, including for the 2016 Trump campaign, and a New York judge ordered Trump to pay $2 million to other charities. The foundation was dissolved.
ethics.outcome: Admitted misuse; ordered to pay $2 million; foundation dissolved.

ethics.title: Georgia 2020 election case
ethics.summary: A Fulton County grand jury indicted Trump and others in 2023 over efforts to overturn Georgia's 2020 election result. After District Attorney Fani Willis was removed from the case, the replacement prosecutor, Peter Skandalakis, asked to drop it, and Judge Scott McAfee dismissed it in its entirety on November 26, 2025.
ethics.outcome: Dismissed at the prosecutor's request; no trial.

ethics.title: Federal 2020 election case (special counsel)
ethics.summary: Special counsel Jack Smith charged Trump in 2023 over efforts to overturn the 2020 election. After Trump won the 2024 election, Smith asked to dismiss the case under Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting president, saying the outcome "is not based on the merits or strength of the case," and Judge Tanya Chutkan dismissed it without prejudice on November 25, 2024.
ethics.outcome: Dismissed without prejudice before trial.

sources.t: WFAE (NPR): Judge grants dismissal of Jan. 6 case against Trump (Nov. 25, 2024)
Axios: Trump's 2020 election interference case dismissed following Jack Smith request

ethics.title: Federal classified documents case (special counsel)
ethics.summary: Trump was charged in 2023 with retaining classified documents and obstructing their return. Judge Aileen Cannon dismissed the case in July 2024, ruling the special counsel's appointment unlawful; the special counsel dropped the appeal as to Trump on November 25, 2024.
ethics.outcome: Dismissed before trial; appeal as to Trump withdrawn.

sources.t: WFAE (NPR): Judge grants dismissal of Jan. 6 case against Trump (covers the classified documents appeal)
Signal (Epoch Times): Special counsel drops Trump election case, classified documents appeal

ethics.title: Second impeachment: incitement of insurrection
ethics.summary: The House impeached Trump on January 13, 2021, on a charge of incitement of insurrection over the January 6 attack. The Senate voted 57–43 to convict on February 13, 2021, short of the two-thirds required, so Trump was acquitted.
ethics.outcome: Acquitted by the Senate, 57–43 (67 votes were needed to convict).

sources.t: U.S. Senate roll call vote 59, 117th Congress (Feb. 13, 2021)
Axios: The Senate acquits Trump (Feb. 13, 2021)

ethics.title: First impeachment: abuse of power and obstruction of Congress
ethics.summary: The House impeached Trump in December 2019 over Trump's dealings with Ukraine. The Senate acquitted Trump on February 5, 2020: 52–48 on abuse of power and 53–47 on obstruction of Congress.
ethics.outcome: Acquitted by the Senate on both articles.

sources.t: Senate Democrats: Roll call vote on impeachment Article I, abuse of power (Feb. 5, 2020)
VOA: U.S. Senate acquits Trump on 2 articles of impeachment

ethics.title: Trump University lawsuits
ethics.summary: Former students' class actions and a New York attorney general suit alleged that Trump University misled students. Trump settled all three for $25 million without admitting wrongdoing; a federal judge gave final approval in April 2018.
ethics.outcome: Settled for $25 million without an admission of wrongdoing.

sources.t: KPBS: Judge finalizes $25 million Trump University settlement (Apr. 9, 2018)
KQED: Judge OKs $25 million settlement of Trump University lawsuit

ethics.title: Foreign emoluments lawsuits
ethics.summary: Maryland, the District of Columbia and hotel and restaurant businesses sued, alleging that payments from foreign and state governments to Trump's businesses violated the Constitution's emoluments clauses. After Trump left office, the Supreme Court vacated the lower-court rulings and ordered the suits dismissed as moot on January 25, 2021, without a ruling on the merits.
ethics.outcome: Dismissed as moot; no ruling on the merits.

sources.t: OPB (AP): Supreme Court ends Trump emoluments lawsuits (Jan. 25, 2021)
